the_kingdom_has_fallen.title: THE KINGDOM HAS FALLEN
the_kingdom_has_fallen.html:
Empress Hou-Ting was killed this morning when a bomb was thrown at her motorcade during the annual celebration of the founding of the Earth Kingdom. The attack set off a night of fighting in Ba Sing Se Square between the city garrison and armed rebels. It ended at 3 a.m., leaving parts of the capital burning, and the city is now under a state of emergency.

The 85th Infantry Division from Omashu was one of the units marching in the square as part of the celebration. Its company commander, Captain Kuvira Beifong, holds dual citizenship in the Qianchan Republic and the Earth Kingdom. She joined the army as a cadet and rose quickly through the ranks.

According to accounts of the fighting, the blast near the Empress’s motorcade killed her and many others and was followed by a firefight on all sides of the square. The rebels carried advanced weapons and explosives, and some used old, mechanized suits left over from the Hundred Year War. They outgunned the garrison near the royal palace. Captain Beifong and her company fought them through the night, and she took the lead in contacting other officers and units to coordinate efforts to retake the city.

Who carried out the attack has not been established. Some sources link it to the Red Lotus or the Equalist movement, which are active in the United Republic and elsewhere. At a military press conference, officials said signs of increased anarchist and Equalist activity had been seen in the weeks before the attack, and that the rebels appeared to have infiltrated the city with agents and weapons. They acknowledged that the military did not act on those warnings.

Why the warnings were missed is unclear. Some sources suggest corruption or collusion within the military ranks, though that is unconfirmed. The public is demanding an investigation and accountability for the security failure.

The succession is undecided, and the Kingdom waits to learn who will rule. Governments abroad are watching closely, fearing that the instability in Ba Sing Se could lead to a civil war.

the_kingdom_is_whole.title: THE KINGDOM IS WHOLE!
the_kingdom_is_whole.html:
Five years to the day after the Earth Queen’s assassination in this square, Generalissimo Kuvira stood on the same spot yesterday and declared the civil war over.

Her armies marched past in ranks that filled the square and spilled into the avenues beyond. Tens of thousands of citizens watched. The parade was unlike any in the Kingdom’s history. Eastern Army regulars marched beside the western divisions that once followed King Shikaei of Omashu. Behind them came republican volunteers, former provincial militias and the mountaineer division that took the northern temples. A year ago these men were in opposing camps. Yesterday they wore one insignia and carried one banner.

“This is not the triumph of one army over another,” said Chen Yulan, The Generalissimo’s spokesman

Speaking from the reviewing stand. “It is the unity of every sector of this nation. The soldier, the farmer, the clerk and the former royalist have agreed that one person can lead them through the rebuilding. They have chosen Kuvira.”

The spokesman said the accord had been reached in recent weeks by representatives of the army, the provincial councils and what he called “the remaining civic bodies of the Kingdom.” He did not say who those bodies were, how they were chosen, or whether a written agreement exists. Asked whether a vote had been held, he said “the people have spoken in the square.”

The Generalissimo addressed the crowd for twelve minutes. She promised bread, roads and a restored capital, and she called the end of the war “the beginning of the work.” She also proclaimed herself Generalissimo Minister of the Earth State, a title she said would remain until “the nation no longer needs a general to hold it together.”

Some observers abroad use a different name. Critics in several capitals have called her the Empress of the Earth Empire, a title they say better fits the powers she has gathered. Government officials rejected the label. “The Earth State has no empress,” said the spokesman. “It has a servant who has chosen to carry a heavy burden.”

Reconstruction crews began clearing the wrecked northern districts this week. Officials say the Harmonist strongholds of the central lands are under control, and the last Equalist positions in the northwest have fallen. Isolated pockets of resistance may remain in the mountain valleys. Authorities are asking citizens to report anyone sheltering armed fugitives.

Foreign delegations attended the ceremony, including envoys from the Qianchan Republic. Their governments have not yet said whether they will recognize the new title.

The Generalissimo left the reviewing stand at dusk. The lamps along the square were lit for the first time since the war began.

generalissimo_or_dictator.title: Generalissimo or Dictator?
generalissimo_or_dictator.html:
Envoys from Qianchan, the Fire Nation and the United Republic sat together at the Victory Day parade, and several said afterward that their governments had weighed an uncomfortable question. Kuvira’s “Earth State” may be the least bad option available.

The question was open on the reviewing stand. The Generalissimo had proclaimed herself Generalissimo Minister, and critics abroad call her an empress in all but name. Her armies were still marching when a Fire Nation attaché said his government “would not welcome a restored crown or a collapsed state and has no other candidates on the table.”

Qianchan’s delegation was led by Deputy Foreign Minister Shen Lihua. Speaking to correspondents afterward, she stressed that attendance did not amount to recognition. “We came to observe,” she said. “We observed an army that is disciplined, a capital that is being fed and a war that has stopped. We also observed that the same person holds the army, the ministries and the ceremony.”

Qianchan’s position has its own history. The Generalissimo is a dual citizen who trained under Qianchan doctrine, and officials in Gaoling have long admitted they are interested in what she becomes. Ms. Shen said that interest was “practical, not sentimental.”

The strongest argument for patience came from the United Republic. Ambassador Teodor Halloran told journalists that the Equalist insurgency has moved into open conflict in Republic City and across the republic’s eastern districts. President Raiko’s government has fought it for months, with Qianchan advisers and supplies helping behind the lines. “A stable Earth Kingdom does not solve our problem,” Mr. Halloran said. “An unstable one hands the insurgents a second front and a refuge.”

Mira Castellan, a correspondent for the Republican Daily who travelled with the delegation, put the dilemma more bluntly. “Every foreign capital here is doing the same sum,” she told this agency. “A strongman who keeps order, or a vacuum the Equalists and the Red Lotus would be glad to use. Nobody is saying she is good. They are saying the alternative is worse.”

The Avatar did not attend. Her aides said she remains in Republic City, occupied with the Equalist crisis, and that she sent no message to the parade. Korra’s absence was noted by delegates; several of whom said an Avatar’s presence might have carried some moral weight to the ceremony.

The Generalissimo’s office produced no evidence of the “agreement among all sectors” it announced. Diplomats said they had been given no written accord or list of signatories. Ms. Shen said her government would “watch what is built, not what is said.”

The delegations leave Ba Sing Se tomorrow. None has announced recognition of the Earth State. None has refused it either.

air_nomad_question.title: Air Nomad Question
air_nomad_question.html:
For most citizens of the United Republic, the Air Nomads have never been a people. They have been a tragedy.

A chapter in a history book. A painting on a classroom wall. A story told by grandparents who themselves never met an airbender. For over a century, the Air Nomads existed in public memory as victims rather than neighbors. Their extermination marked the beginning of the Hundred Year War and, for many years, its most enduring symbol. Yet symbols are easier to preserve than people.

Now, only months after the passing of Avatar Aang, that reality appears to be changing.

Over recent weeks this newspaper has confirmed reports of Air Nomad descendants, affiliated spiritual communities, Air Acolytes, and families claiming ancestral ties to the old nomad routes arriving on Air Temple Island from every corner of the world. Some come from the Fire Nation. Others arrive from remote Earth Kingdom provinces, the Water Tribes, and settlements throughout the United Republic. Some bear documented family histories. Others carry little more than oral traditions passed down through generations.

For the first time since the war, the possibility has emerged that the Air Nomads may survive not merely as a memory, but as a living community.

The gathering is modest in size. Its significance is not. That prospect has revived an old argument.

What, precisely, happened to them? And why has the world spent more than 150 years avoiding a clear answer?

A Question Older Than the Republic

The phrase "Air Nomad Genocide" is common today. It was not always so.

During the war, Imperial publications referred to the destruction of the temples as military operations. Official statements spoke of eliminating the Avatar threat and suppressing hostile elements. The language was bureaucratic, distant, and carefully chosen.

Even after the war, many governments preferred ambiguity. The Earth Kingdom, exhausted by invasion and civil collapse, focused on reconstruction. The Water Tribes honored the dead but possessed little documentary evidence. The Fire Nation's archives remained largely closed. Historians argued. Politicians deferred. The public moved on.

The result was a strange consensus. Everyone agreed the Air Nomads had disappeared. Few wished to discuss why.

The Facts We Know

There are, despite persistent claims to the contrary, certain facts that are no longer seriously disputed. The four Air Temples were attacked in coordinated operations. The assaults occurred at the outset of the war. The overwhelming majority of Air Nomads present at the temples were killed. The ancient institutions of Air Nomad society ceased to function afterward. No organized Air Nomad government, monastic order, or successor state survived. The Air Nomads, as a people, effectively vanished from world affairs.

Reasonable historians may debate numbers. They may debate planning, logistics, responsibility, and the degree to which individual commanders understood the scope of the operation. What becomes increasingly difficult to debate is the outcome. A culture that had existed for thousands of years was reduced to a handful of survivors. Among them was Avatar Aang. For generations, the world's understanding of the Air Nomads was largely mediated through a single man.

Now he, too, is gone.

The Weight of a Word

The disagreement centers on one word. Genocide.

There are those, particularly among conservative circles in the Fire Nation, who object to the term. They argue it imposes contemporary moral standards upon a distant conflict. Some insist the objective was military rather than ethnic. Others contend that the destruction of the temples, however catastrophic, does not prove an intention to eliminate an entire people.

These arguments deserve consideration. They have also been made for more than a century. Against them stands a simple fact: When the campaign began, there were Air Nomads. When it ended, there were not. If the deliberate destruction of a people does not constitute genocide, then words have lost their meaning.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW

Some readers may ask why this debate should be reopened at all. The war is long over. The perpetrators and victims are almost entirely gone. The world faces newer problems. The answer can be found on Air Temple Island. History is never merely about the dead. It is also about the living.

The young men and women arriving on the island today are not responsible for the crimes of the past. Nor are they merely custodians of someone else's memory. They are attempting to decide what it means to belong to a people that the world once assumed had vanished forever.

Their task is difficult enough without inherited falsehoods.

where_the_war_ended.title: Where the war ended?
where_the_war_ended.html:
Ask ten people between the Outer Wall and the Yanakawan coast where the Hundred Year War ended, and you will receive ten different answers.

To the Imperial Diet in Caldera City, it ended when the high command radio broadcast four words at 12:27 PM on July 18, 100 AG. To the diplomats who signed the parchment at Qinglan Port five years later, it ended on April 28, 105 AG. To the farmers of the central plains, who spent the last thirteen years dodging provincial warlords and stray demobilized battalions, it didn't end until last summer, when the joint pacification columns from Omashu and Gaoling finally seized the last illegal arsenals.

Thirteen years after the sky turned white over the Western District, the geography of peace remains a matter of perspective.

The Wall

At the Western Outer Wall, where the masonry still looks lighter than the centuries-old stone surrounding it, Bao Zhen does not care about calendar dates.

Bao, 54, is a stonemason. On July 17, 100 AG, he was standing on a scaffolding two miles south of the breach when the Imperial Sōen array discharged. He lost the sight in his left eye to the flash; his elder brother was among the 380,000 who died in the blast wave and the firestorms that followed.

"People from the inner rings come out here on the eighteenth of July to lay white lilies," Bao says, setting a chisel against a granite block. He speaks without looking up. "They call today the anniversary of the end. But the war didn't end on the eighteenth. On the eighteenth, the sky was still full of black dust, the radio was dead, and we were pulling people out of the rubble with our bare hands. For us, the war didn't end when the Fire Lord fell. It ended three weeks later when the fires finally went out and the water mains stopped running red."

Four miles away, in the Upper Ring, King Kuei’s administrative offices present a different timeline. Clerks sit behind stacks of census ledgers, trying to count a population that was fractured by a century of foreign invasion and twelve years of internal anarchy.

Under the Crown’s ongoing civil reforms, land titles are slowly being restored to survivors, and the universal franchise enacted before the royal centralizing decrees remains nominally on track. But the bureaucratic machinery moves with excruciating weight. In the ledger offices, the war is recorded as a series of open files—millions of missing persons whose legal status cannot be resolved because the parish records in the provinces were burned by warlord militias in 104 AG.

The Road to the Coast

South along the Grand Trunk Road toward the former frontline zones, the memory of 100 AG melts into the more recent scars of the Post-War Conflicts.

In the market town of Hanxu, on the edge of the Si Wong Desert, the ruins of Imperial fuel depots sit beside low-slung concrete barracks built during the warlord era. Here, the end of the war is not marked by the death of an Emperor, but by the departure of General Sheng’s rogue regional division in 112 AG.

"When the Fire Lord died in Qinglan, nothing changed for us," says Lin Fen, who runs a dry-goods stall near the former rail cut. She points to a rusted shell casing being used as a hitching post outside her shop. "The Imperial troops marched out, but the provincial commanders took their place the next week. They wanted our grain just the same. They used the same rifles. They called themselves 'Protectors of the Realm,' but they stole our pigs and burned our barns just like the soldiers in red did."

To Lin, the war lasted one hundred and twelve years. "It ended last November," she says flatly, "when the Gaoling militia came through and hanged the last three tax-collectors who didn't have a seal from the King or the Republic."

Qinglan Port

Four hundred miles to the west, across the boundary of the United Republic of Nations, Qinglan Port looks nothing like the ruined staging ground where Avatar Aang brought down Fire Lord Ozai.

Today, Qinglan is a sprawling, smoke-plumed port of iron-framed warehouses, electric tramways, and mixed neighborhoods where former Imperial Navy conscripts live in the same apartment blocks as Earth Kingdom refugees. Freight steamers fly the four-element banner of the United Republic, carrying machinery to Caldera and timber to Ba Sing Se.

On the granite pier where the Imperial Sōen array once stood, a bronze plaque marks the site of the July 18 engagement.

"This is where it ended," says Lan Shuyi, a former captain in the Yanakawan Liberation Front who now works as a dock foreman. He sits on a wooden crate, nursing a cup of cold tea. "You can ask the lawyers in Republic City who point to the 105 AG Treaty of Qinglan, but they weren't here when the firing stopped. At 12:27 PM, when the radio said 'The Emperor is dead,' half the Imperial garrison dropped their weapons and started crying. The other half started shooting at their own officers. That was the moment the Empire died."

Yet half a mile down the quay, in a tavern frequented by Fire Nation veterans who stayed in Yanakawa after the capitulation, the answer changes again.

"The war didn't end in Qinglan," says Takeda, 58, a former mechanist in the 37th Armored Division who lost his right arm at Ba Sing Se. He stares out at the harbor, where a Qianchan freighter is unloading coal. "Qinglan was just the day the high command collapsed. For us in the islands, the war went on for eighteen years in the volcanic hills while Zuko and Azula fought over the ashes. My home village was burned in 108 AG by Salvationist deserters—eight years after Ozai died."

A Peace of Fragments

As the sun sets over the broad, flat plains of the central Earth Kingdom, the reconstruction efforts continue under a gray sky.

King Kuei’s ministers report progress: municipal elections have been scheduled in three more southern districts for next spring, and the joint boundary commissions between Ba Sing Se and the United Republic have completed two hundred miles of survey work without major incident.

Yet drive through any village between the capital and the sea, and the illusion of a single, clean historical narrative dissolves.

The Hundred Year War did not end with a single stroke of a pen or a single fall of a spear. It ended in pieces—in a burned-out bunker in Qinglan, on a blood-soaked parade ground in Omashu, in a quiet room in Gaoling when a treaty was signed, and in thousands of forgotten hamlets when the last deserter ran out of ammunition.

In a small graveyard outside the rebuilt walls of Yu Dao, an old woman sweeps dead leaves from a row of unmarked stone slabs. When asked which year the peace began, she pauses, leaning on her broom.

"I don't know when it ended," she says, turning back to the stones. "I only know who didn't come home."

To Lin, the war lasted one hundred and twelve years. "It ended last November," she says flatly, "when the Gaoling militia came through and hanged the last three tax-collectors who didn't have a seal from the King or the Republic."

---

## Qinglan Port

Four hundred miles to the west, across the boundary of the United Republic of Nations, Qinglan Port looks nothing like the ruined staging ground where Avatar Aang brought down Fire Lord Ozai.

Today, Qinglan is a sprawling, smoke-plumed port of iron-framed warehouses, electric tramways, and mixed neighborhoods where former Imperial Navy conscripts live in the same apartment blocks as Earth Kingdom refugees. Freight steamers fly the four-element banner of the United Republic, carrying machinery to Caldera and timber to Ba Sing Se.

On the granite pier where the Imperial Sōen array once stood, a bronze plaque marks the site of the July 18 engagement.

"This is where it ended," says Lan Shuyi, a former captain in the Yanakawan Liberation Front who now works as a dock foreman. He sits on a wooden crate, nursing a cup of cold tea. "You can ask the lawyers in Republic City who point to the 105 AG Treaty of Qinglan, but they weren't here when the firing stopped. At 12:27 PM, when the radio said 'The Emperor is dead,' half the Imperial garrison dropped their weapons and started crying. The other half started shooting at their own officers. That was the moment the Empire died."

Yet half a mile down the quay, in a tavern frequented by Fire Nation veterans who stayed in Yanakawa after the capitulation, the answer changes again.

"The war didn't end in Qinglan," says Takeda, 58, a former mechanist in the 37th Armored Division who lost his right arm at Ba Sing Se. He stares out at the harbor, where a Qianchan freighter is unloading coal. "Qinglan was just the day the high command collapsed. For us in the islands, the war went on for eighteen years in the volcanic hills while Zuko and Azula fought over the ashes. My home village was burned in 108 AG by Salvationist deserters—eight years after Ozai died."

---

## A Peace of Fragments

As the sun sets over the broad, flat plains of the central Earth Kingdom, the reconstruction efforts continue under a gray sky.

King Kuei’s ministers report progress: municipal elections have been scheduled in three more southern districts for next spring, and the joint boundary commissions between Ba Sing Se and the United Republic have completed two hundred miles of survey work without major incident.

Yet drive through any village between the capital and the sea, and the illusion of a single, clean historical narrative dissolves.

The Hundred Year War did not end with a single stroke of a pen or a single fall of a spear. It ended in pieces—in a burned-out bunker in Qinglan, on a blood-soaked parade ground in Omashu, in a quiet room in Gaoling when a treaty was signed, and in thousands of forgotten hamlets when the last deserter ran out of ammunition.

In a small graveyard outside the rebuilt walls of Yu Dao, an old woman sweeps dead leaves from a row of unmarked stone slabs. When asked which year the peace began, she pauses, leaning on her broom.

"I don't know when it ended," she says, turning back to the stones. "I only know who didn't come home."
